Pokemon Childhood Version: A romhack where Mew is under the truck
items.summary: assembly, games
items.content:
TL;DR I made a romhack which implements the most common urban legends from the gen 1 Pokemon games.

The old fashioned way! I did not make the actual getting to the truck any easier. You have to either trade for a Pokemon that knows CUT, to avoid entering the S.S. Anne. Or, you can enter the ship and collect the CUT HM as usual, then backtrack to a trainer on the ship that you have not already defeated, battle them, and let them win. This will teleport you back to the nearest Pokecentre without triggering the S.S. Anne to leave.

I don't want to host the rom directly because Nintendo will eviscerate me. What I have below is a patching tool: select an original, unmodified ROM file that you ripped from your personal copy you've had since you were twelve, and it will patch it, and save the modified version. Under no circumstances should you use a ROM file ripped by anyone else, because that would be very naughty.

Select your Pokemon Red or Blue (USA, Europe) ROM to patch:

Source code available on github . Thanks to the pret/pokered contributors, without whose hard labour this would not have been possible. Also BTW I actually tried the Mew under the truck thing when I was a kid. I was devastated when it didn't work. Satisfaction at long last.

items.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
items.summary: browsers, ios
items.content:
Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
items.content:
Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.

To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.

We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.

Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.

By default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.

With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:

In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.

In just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.

After 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “ Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions” . This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.

Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any issues, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?

Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads.

With Ternary Bonsai 2 27B , we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately.

Agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an important milestone in improving the intelligence density of models.

Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical.

I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is

items.title: Microsoft’s historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”: Internal memos reveal a “Code Red” overhaul and ambitious one-hour recovery goals.
items.content:
According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

Amanda Silver , a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ, wrote that engineers had to contend with a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. According to Silver, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, leaving diagnostic data scattered, and a full view of the incident fractured. Silver’s memo also quotes Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, telling a Code Red review that the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”

Microsoft has said the outage was not related to any cyberattack or malicious activity, and the defects were not caused by AI tooling.  As part of the Code Red overhaul, Silver’s memo outlines five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. According to Reuters, Microsoft plans to improve its incident response and patching timelines by deploying its own AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said that he will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering team responsible for Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft has set targets of one-hour worldwide resolution in major incidents and a one-hour deployment window for urgent security fixes. It hasn’t said when it hopes to meet them, or how future response efforts will avoid 11 separate Teams chats and the “fog of war.”

items.title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, stuff
items.summary: c++, java, performance
items.content:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.

Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.

It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.

SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.

The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction,

possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;

I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations.

Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search

because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos.

Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately?

I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from,

how many users I have, or what they’re up to.

At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet,

but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.

On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,

you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.

I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key,

I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key,

and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to,

and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual

copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again

(ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good

part of my career helping people streamline and automate).

Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.

I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go,

in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement,

but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax,

and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.

Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward

and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms

that already exists for on-heap structures but not off;

bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow,

Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine,

performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.

To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact,

and if we do I doubt it will be massive , as the Java implementation is already very optimized,

and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.

Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor…

Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Scientists Create a 'Planimal' by Fusing Hamster And Algae DNA
items.content:
Scientists Create a 'Planimal' by Fusing Hamster And Algae DNA

Nature 21 November 2026 By Jess Cockerill

'Planimal' cell chromosomes. (© Sachihiro Matsunaga, The University of Tokyo 2026)

Long before humans were collaging the genomes of different species together, nature was doing it on its own .

Now, biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga from the University of Tokyo has led a team in encouraging algal DNA to merge with the chromosomes in hamster cells, producing a hybrid genome that persists across more than 150 generations of cell division.

The results are published in Nature Communications.

They call it a 'planimal', a portmanteau of plant and animal which Matsunaga first conceived in 2018 , to refer to artificial animal cells that are fused with algae to give them plant-like traits – namely, photosynthesis.

Matsunaga's plans for these cells are lofty.

In his 2018 paper, he said planimal cells will one day "contribute to overcoming global food problems by reducing energy consumption", "enable photosynthetic therapies" for medical applications, and "support migration to other planets under the harsh conditions through long-distance space travel".

Theoretically, such a cell could harness sunlight in-house to produce the oxygen and sugars that the animal parts of it need to survive.

It sounds like science fiction, but it's actually already happening on our own planet, without any human involvement.

Back in 2000 , scientists actually discovered such an organism on a sandy beach at Isonoura in Wakayama, Japan.

They named the single-celled eukaryote Hatena arenicola .

It spends half of its life as a 'plant', thanks to an intimate symbiosis with the photosynthetic algae Nephroselmis , which lives inside the Hatena cell.

Their merger seems to be quite a lot further along than other examples you might've heard of . The algae's chloroplasts are greatly enlarged, while the rest of its cellular 'organs' are degraded.

Scientists agree that plants got their ability to photosynthesize through a similar process.

It was the ancient origin of chloroplasts, and the strange organism Hatena, that inspired Matsunaga.

Now, in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Japan and Australia, he has realized his synthetic 'planimal' cells in a lab and watched them carry the algal genes across multiple generations of asexual cell division.

"We have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal, and have shown that this genetic material can be stably passed on to daughter cells through repeated cell divisions," he says.

This microscope image captures the fusion of the red alga cell (seen here in green) with the much larger, transparent cultured animal cell. The other small green spheres are algal cells, while the large transparent cell below is another animal cell. ( © Sachihiro Matsunaga, The University of Tokyo 2026 ) They didn't use typical genetic modification methods: they used lab techniques to force the cells to follow pathways inspired by endosymbiosis.

One of those pathways is phagocytosis, in which the animal cell engulfed the algal cell. That's a natural process: all the researchers had to do was put the animal and algal cells in the same container and wait.

This method worked, and even produced some stable cell lines, but the success rate was extremely low: only 3.7 colonies formed for every 1.2 × 10⁷ cells.

An artificial route proved more effective.

The scientists bathed the hamster and algae cells in polyethylene glycol, which jumbled their cell membranes just enough to get the two different species to fuse.

The yield from this method was about 800 times greater than letting phagocytosis do the work.

To be sure the algal DNA was properly integrated into the hamster cell genomes, it also needs to survive cell replication across generations.

items.title: 2035 came early
items.summary: nix, wasm
items.content:
tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox .

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript.

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev .

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev .

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability.

I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix .

It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster.  especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Chrome prerendering is weird
items.content:
Here’s something I learned at work recently: when you type in Chrome’s address bar, Chrome may load the top suggestion in the background before you press Enter. It isn’t just a DNS lookup or a fetch of the HTML. The page is fully prerendered: JavaScript runs, and anything it writes to localStorage stays written, even if you never visit the page. This isn’t a bug: it’s documented behaviour , designed to make navigation feel instant.

This caused a problem in the onboarding flow at Synthesia, where I work. It took me a long time to pin down because it only happened intermittently, and - for reasons I’ll explain - never when I was actively watching for it .

When someone signs up for Synthesia, the flow they see depends on which landing page they came from. We use query parameters to tailor onboarding to a particular product or use case.

Those parameters only exist on the first URL loaded by the application. Once the user proceeds through the sign-up steps, they’re long gone. So on first load, the app takes a snapshot of the query string and saves it to localStorage . Later, when the account is created, it sends that snapshot to the backend, which picks the onboarding flow.

The snapshot is only taken once. If there’s already one in storage, the app leaves it alone. Once onboarding is completed, the snapshot is cleared.

Some colleagues testing specific onboarding flows would occasionally get the wrong one. They’d open a fresh Incognito window, visit a landing page configured to send some specific parameters, sign up, and get the wrong journey. Then when I tried to reproduce the bug myself, it would work fine. This went on for months, and began to drive me crazy.

After a mammoth debugging session with Claude, I finally figured out what was happening:

They open an Incognito window and start typing synt… into the address bar.

Chrome suggests a page in the app they’ve visited before - like their recent videos - and highlights it.

Chrome is confident enough that they’ll go there that it prerenders the page in the background.

The app loads in that invisible page, grabs any parameters from the URL, and saves them in localStorage .

The user carries on typing the URL they actually wanted - or modifies one of Chrome’s suggested URLs - with the right parameters.

They hit Enter, land on the marketing site, and prepare to test the sign-up journey.

They click through to sign up. The app loads with the right parameters, finds a snapshot already in localStorage , and leaves it alone.

From then on, every page in that Incognito session uses the wrong snapshot . Even though the app was opened with the correct parameters, Chrome had already loaded a different URL in the background and effectively poisoned localStorage with a different set of parameters.

Chrome autocompleting a page I visit a lot. By this point, it may already be prerendering it.

Note that Incognito doesn’t protect you here. It starts with an empty localStorage , but that storage is shared by every tab in the Incognito session, and that includes Chrome’s invisible prerendered ones 🫠. And the address bar suggestions in Incognito are based on your normal browsing history, so Chrome still knows where you’re likely to go.

Two things made this bug almost impossible to catch in the act:

It doesn’t happen with DevTools open. Chrome’s omnibox refuses to prerender a suggestion in any tab that has DevTools open, a check added back in 2019 . Nothing shows in DevTools Speculative loads panel either. The moment I opened the Application tab to watch, the bug went away. Schrödinger’s localStorage 🐈

It doesn’t happen in a fresh browser profile. With no history there’s nothing to suggest, and nothing to prerender. Pasting a correct URL into the address bar skips the problem too.

Security incident on Hex.pm
items.summary: elixir, erlang, gleam
items.content:
On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability.

We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs.

Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm . Please forward suspicious emails to security@hex.pm .

We checked every file written to package storage during the incident against our database and found nothing unexpected. Reads of private packages in that period came from our own servers and coincide with releases the same organizations published at the time. A read made from a compromised server would look like one of ours, so we can't fully rule one out, and reads of private documentation aren't logged. We will contact affected organizations directly.

The attacker's commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients. We're building a new registry signing system that supports key rotation, with new Hex client releases in the coming days. Until then, don't trust third-party mirrors and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm. We already deployed fixes for the vulnerability and are working on further hardening fixes.

Reset your 2FA at hex.pm/dashboard/security : under "Authenticator App", choose "Setup New App" and verify a code from the new entry. You get a new secret and new recovery codes, so store the new codes. This works when an organization requires 2FA, where disabling it is refused.

Update your Hex client when the release with the new signing system is out in the coming days. Until then, use only repo.hex.pm, not mirrors. To update, run mix local.hex --force , and update rebar3 or Gleam if you use them.

18:16 - 18:29 : The attacker sent 69 malicious requests to hex.pm, six of our web servers were affected. Our error tracker Sentry recorded its first error at 18:16:00 and recorded an error for each request.

18:27 : We added a firewall rule to block the attacker's traffic, which took full effect between 18:30 and 18:33.

18:30 - 18:31 : All hex.pm servers were replaced with a patched build that rejects these payloads.

18:33 - 18:38 : All further requests from the attacking address were denied.

18:35 : We began investigating production logs and the database.

18:49 : We deactivated the AWS access key the affected servers used, after creating a replacement at 18:47.

19:07 : We received an email with a security report that described the same vulnerability.

20:21 : Most infrastructure credentials were rotated. The database password followed on November 24.

22:58 : We reported a personal data breach to IMY, the Swedish data protection authority.

23:05 : We reported the incident to CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which confirmed receipt at 23:43.

23:26 : We submitted an early warning to ENISA, the EU Agency for Cybersecurity.

By 10:42 : We had rotated every credential the attacker could have read, including the database password, except the registry signing key and a few low-impact secrets.

The vulnerability in Hex.pm is tracked as CVE-2026-129514 .

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
items.content:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500 .

2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.

Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested

2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.

Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie

Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.

2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

items.title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found 17 unreported bugs
items.summary: clojure
items.content:
I read Koukyosyumei's article " 著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話 " (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs").

The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain.

Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples.

I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org.

They include reduce on vector-of , the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries.

The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21.

The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition.

You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32 , the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations.

So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of % .

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code.

I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property.

Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results.

For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level.

The operations were conj , pop , assoc , and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before.

I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays.

Clojure implements it in gvec.clj , written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector .

If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65504 ))))

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65505 ))))

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( vec ( range 65505 ))))

The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj , where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

( recur result ( bit-and 0xffe0 ( + aidx 32 )))

The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it.

With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504.

After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce .

On Monday morning, just before markets opened, Nvidia’s board of directors announced that it unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and director—only 11 days after it had fired him over reports of an inappropriate workplace affair, as well as a potentially compromising romantic and business relationship with a likely Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation).

“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s announcement reads in part. “Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

This occurred just one day after the New York Times confirmed that Alice Huang had regular contact with an official in China’s Ministry of State Security while she and Nvidia’s Taiwanese-origin CEO were together, and while she was receiving Nvidia chips on behalf of a regime that was not supposed to have access to them. The board said on Monday that an independent committee would continue to investigate the possible Chinese intelligence plot, while Nvidia installs more guardrails over trade law and national security. (The Securities and Exchange Commission is also continuing a probe into Nvidia’s accounting disclosures.)

If anything’s clear now, it’s that Jensen Huang and his pals in the White House are gonna keep running things the way they like—which is just fine by the stock markets, which saw massive relief this morning after all the drubbing it took following Huang’s initial ouster. It’ll also be fine by Big Tech, whose leaders consistently advocated for Huang over the past week even as the Times published stories from subordinates who decried the CEO’s allegedly abusive management style .

However, the American people might not be fine with it—especially after registering their displeasure at the ballot box with President Donald Trump’s corruption and the aggressive nature of the A.I. boom. If you’re wondering whether the “input from senior levels of the United States government” in Nvidia’s statement was a euphemism for Trump, the commander in chief all but appeared to confirm that himself on Monday.

“I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump said to CNBC when asked if he thought Huang would have been rehired without his intervention.

Tech Oversight Project CEO Sacha Haworth wrote in a statement that “this whole ordeal only reinforces what Americans already believe about a broken political system that stands up for Big Tech CEOs and not the American people.” Tech lawyer Eugene Rome points out that Nvidia’s ongoing investigations indicate that “this wasn’t driven by a final answer on the spy affair. As Gasparino previously revealed , the primary means by which Huang and his supporters hoped to persuade Nvidia’s board to bring him back was by undermining Alice Huang’s known status as a potential national security risk. items.title: KDE and GNOME Desktop: A Detailed Comparison. Why I Still Choose KDE?
items.content:
This article discusses why I, Ivon, prefer KDE Plasma over GNOME as my Linux desktop. I will try to first compare the differences between the two from an objective angle, then transition into extremely subjective personal opinions.

Current Linux distributions offer more than 20 desktop environments for users to choose from, and the largest groups are “GNOME” and “KDE Plasma.” From the image below, you can see that their design languages differ enormously.

Thanks to Linux’s high degree of freedom, Linux can have multiple desktop environments coexist, but most people get used to using the desktop installed when they install the system, right? The same applies to “Arch Linux”, whose installation process requires self-assembly.

The desktop environment largely determines the experience of using a Linux computer, so choosing a desktop that suits you is very important.

I have installed Linux on different computers and tried both GNOME and KDE Plasma desktops. After several years of repeated comparison, I reached my future preference for desktop environments: if I distro-hop, KDE Plasma takes priority, with GNOME second. In other words, when installing a desktop environment, KDE Plasma is always the main choice.

Source: https://www.reddit.com/r/linuxmasterrace/comments/tj03r4/totally_unbiased_meme_that_isnt_going_to_make/

The GNOME and KDE desktops mentioned here both refer to “unmodified original” vanilla versions. Heavily patched ones like Ubuntu are not included.

Let’s start with an interesting statistic. The Arch Linux official website tracks desktop environment package installations, and we can see that KDE downloads gradually surpassed GNOME and XFCE after 2018.

1. Brief Introduction to GNOME and KDE Plasma

First, let me explain why I only consider GNOME and KDE Plasma: watermelon leans toward the bigger side (Si-kue uá tuā pîng). Things used by many people can receive the most timely support. I know Linux has other desktop environments, but sorry, this article will not discuss them.

Next, let’s talk about market share. GNOME and KDE Plasma are both desktop environments with long histories. GNOME released its first version in 1999, while KDE released in 1998. Later, KDE became the code name of a large project, so when discussing the desktop environment, the name KDE Plasma is used. From here, we can observe that KDE was developed earlier than GNOME!

But early KDE made developers wary because QT’s license terms were not free enough. Trolltech’s earliest QT version used the FreeQt License, which was incompatible with free software licenses. Because most KDE components were written with QT, relying on components with licensing problems was dangerous and could create unnecessary legal issues. This indirectly promoted the birth of GNOME, which mainly used GTK for development and adopted the GPL license. Major companies then adopted GNOME as their main desktop environment. However, after QT later revised its terms, the licensing problem disappeared, and the KDE Plasma desktop license became a mixture of GPL + LGPL + BSD. Now both desktop environments are free software and have no licensing issue.

Possibly because of the licensing factor above, as time passed, more than half of commercial Linux distributions on the market adopted GNOME as the default desktop, including Ubuntu, RHEL, SUSE Linux, and System76 Pop!_OS. Therefore, saying GNOME is the face of Linux systems is not an exaggeration.

A common saying is that GNOME’s code is maintained not only by the civilian open source community, but also supported by major commercial companies such as RedHat and SUSE. They use GNOME as the desktop for their own commercial distributions, which may be deployed on critical servers, so developers will not casually ruin the project (?) The GNOME desktop should theoretically be very stable, or else why would commercial companies trust it so much?

items.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
items.content:
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Had at Least 4 Affairs
items.content:
Quantifying some business guy’s sex life may not be classy work, but newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs have the power to move trillions of dollars in shareholder value around. To paraphrase New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , this guy’s libido determines whether or not a lot of people will ever get to retire, so we all deserve to know how many affairs there were.

And the answer, according to the Wall Street Journal’s latest anonymously sourced report on the AI chip company, is at least four . At least .

During an hours-long meeting of the Nvidia board on Sunday, the Journal writes, Huang told the board about “additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported.” The report is attributed to “people with knowledge of the discussion.”

Three alleged affairs have been widely reported . Huang has publicly acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have been spying on behalf of the Chinese government , but there were two other alleged relationships with Nvidia employees as well. At any rate, whatever the Journal’s report considers “additional affairs beyond the two,” the use of the plural “affairs” means the board has heard about four at minimum.

Huang resigned on November 12 , then for over a week, tech stocks teetered , and then amid an SEC probe of Nvidia, plunged on Friday , sparking fears that the AI bubble had officially burst .

President Trump, a personal friend of Huang’s, has insisted that Huang did “ nothing wrong .” Trump did, however, post a meme on Truth Social on Monday—shortly after Huang’s reinstatement—showing a bloodied Huang posed with his fist in the air like Trump after his 2024 assassination attempt, holding aloft a bra .

On Monday, after Huang’s return, Nvidia gained back $990 billion in market value , reportedly the largest single-day gain for a U.S. company in history.

The Journal’s report says Huang was contrite about the additional affairs. During a speech to employees on Monday, he thanked them and told them he would be a “better CEO the second time around.”

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: What runs your JavaScript? Engines, runtimes, and why there are so many
items.content:
Most people who write JavaScript run it in a browser tab or with node file.js . But JavaScript runs in far more places than those two. There are engines built for microcontrollers with mere kilobytes of memory; engines written in Rust, Go, and Java to sit inside programs in those languages; an engine written in JavaScript itself; and compilers that turn JavaScript into a native binary with no engine in it at all. The JavaScript engines zoo catalogs more than a hundred of them. [1]

This post is the vocabulary for that list: what an engine is, what a runtime is, and why there are so many of both.

JavaScript is defined by a document, not by a program or a single reference implementation.

JavaScript's formal name is ECMAScript (ES), and it's defined by a specification , ECMA-262 . TC39 ( Ecma International 's Technical Committee 39) writes it in the open on GitHub , and (these days) Ecma publishes a dated edition annually. The current one is ECMAScript 2026, the 17th edition. [2]

Next to the specification sits test262 , the official test suite: over 50,000 small tests for the language and its internationalization API. [3] TC39 maintains the two as separate things. One says what the language is, and the other checks an implementation against it. Many engines implement the specification and test themselves against the suite.

One definition, many implementations: none of them is the reference; each answers to the same document.

Things didn't start off this way. In the beginning, there was only one implementation: Mocha (later LiveScript ), written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995. The language was renamed JavaScript in December 1995 and shipped in Netscape Navigator 2.0 the following March. Meanwhile, folks at Microsoft were working on what would become JScript —in essence, Internet Explorer's answer to Netscape's JavaScript. Within the language's first year, according to Allen Wirfs-Brock and Brendan Eich's history of it, web developers were already "encountering interoperability issues between Netscape's JavaScript and Microsoft's reverse-engineered implementation." [4] Two browsers, two engines, and pages that behaved differently in each. Standardization began at Ecma International in 1996, and the first standard, under the name ECMAScript, came out in 1997. [4:1] The timeline below runs from there to ESNext (the informal name for whatever comes next). [5]

Implementation first, specification after: the language began as whatever Netscape shipped, and ECMA-262 came later to settle a single definition. ECMAScript editions, ES for short, were numbered up to the sixth, which was also the first named by year, ES2015. Sources: Wirfs-Brock and Eich ; Ecma, ECMA-262 ; tc39.es/ecma262 .

For the fuller story, there's Wirfs-Brock and Eich's paper itself; [4:2] and Deno 's "A brief history of JavaScript," which covers much more than the editions: browsers, runtimes, and tooling. [6]

For some languages, the main implementation effectively is the language. Rust has a specification team, and, in 2025, the Rust project adopted a specification, the FLS (originally the Ferrocene Language Specification). But the FLS describes Rust "as implemented by the Rust compiler (rustc)," and, when in doubt, it "prefers documenting behavior of rustc over claiming correctness as a specification." [7]

JavaScript isn't like that. No engine is JavaScript. Most of us use more than one engine in a day: V8 in Chrome on a laptop, JavaScriptCore in Safari on a phone. Any program that runs JavaScript the way ECMA-262 describes (conforms to the specification) is a JavaScript engine—whatever it's written in, however small it is, and wherever it runs.

JavaScript isn't alone in that shape. C has a standard, ISO/IEC 9899; and many compilers, among them GCC (the GNU Compiler Collection) and Clang . SQL has one too, ISO/IEC 9075; and many databases that each implement it a little differently. [8] Rust isn't the only language defined in practice by one…
